title: Secrets Management
summary: Secrets management is the discipline of storing, distributing, rotating and auditing the credentials that systems use to authenticate to each other, such as API keys, database passwords, certificates and signing keys. The core idea is that a secret should live in one controlled store, be delivered to a workload at run time rather than baked into an image or a repository, and be replaced on a schedule or on suspicion without editing application code. In a container platform this appears as an external secret store reached through a workload identity, short lived tokens injected as files or environment variables, and audit records that show which workload read which secret. The mistake that keeps recurring is putting a secret in a container image, a build variable or a manifest held in version control, because the value is then copied into every registry layer, build log and developer machine, and rotation becomes impossible to complete.

beginner.definition: Secrets management means looking after the passwords and keys that software uses to talk to other software. A secret is any value that must stay private, such as an API key or a database password. A good system keeps secrets in one safe place, gives them out only when needed, and changes them often.
beginner.whyItMatters: A stolen secret lets an attacker act as your application. If the secret sits in code or in an image, copies spread everywhere and nobody can track them. Changing it then means rebuilding and redeploying many systems. A central store makes rotation quick and gives you a record of use. It also removes the need to share passwords between people by hand.
howItWorks: A secret is created in a central store, which encrypts it and records who may read it.
A workload proves its identity with a token or certificate from the platform, not with a password.
The store checks that identity against its policy and returns only the secrets it allows.
The secret is delivered at run time, often as a file that lives in memory only.
The store rotates the secret on a schedule, and the workload picks up the new value.
Every read is logged, so unusual access from a strange workload becomes visible.
beginner.example: Picture an office where every door has a different key. Instead of giving each worker a heavy ring of keys, the front desk lends one key. The desk checks your badge first and hands over only what you need. The key is returned at the end of the task, and the desk writes down the loan. If a key is lost, the desk changes that lock only. Secrets management is that front desk system.
takeaways: Keep secrets in one controlled store, not in code, images, or build variables.
Give each workload an identity so it can fetch its secrets at run time.
Rotate secrets on a schedule and keep a record of every read.

objectives: Explain what counts as a secret and why it needs special handling.
Describe how a workload identity allows secrets to be fetched at run time.
Explain the risks of storing secrets inside images or version control.
Outline how rotation limits the value of a leaked credential.
Recognise how audit logs of secret access support detection.
